fetched_contents.text: A comprehensive review of the influence of co-solvents on the catalysed methanolysis process to obtain biodiesel Abstract Non-polar oil and polar short-chain alcohols, used as reactants in the transesterification reaction, are immiscible. Transesterification reactions can only occur on the phase boundary and they are therefore diffusion-limited. Several methods are employed to overcome the limitation of mass transfer by increasing miscibility and thereby accelerating the reaction. Co-solvents are additional solvents that should be soluble in the oil and alcohol phase; this could lead to an increase in the reaction rate and a reduction in the temperature and the reaction time. This work aims to provide a comprehensive literature review on the influence of co-solvents on the processes of catalysed methanolysis for the biodiesel production. Most authors have not systematically determined and justified the effects of cosolvents. So far it seems impossible to establish which cosolvents are the most suitable for which methanolysis systems. The purpose of this work is to highlight and justify the differences or similarities in co-solvent impacts among the various publications by examining the chemical structure of the respective co-solvents, including the functional groups and the resulting physicochemical properties such as the dielectric constant or the log P value. Besides biodiesel, co-solvents like THF and acetone seems to be the best choices for alkaline methanolysis systems due to successful broadly applications with different oils, catalysts and reaction conditions. Moreover, THF and n-hexane are essentially advisable for in-situ methanolysis. Keywords: Biodiesel biofuel, Catalysis, Co-solvent, Mass transfer, Methanolysis Highlights * • Effect of co-solvent on the catalysed methanolysis. * • Co-solvents to overcome the mass transfer limitation. * • Advances in the use of co-solvents for the biodiesel production. Introduction Biodiesel is a non-petroleum-based fuel for use in compression ignition engines that comprises of mono-alkyl esters of long chain fatty acids derived from vegetable oils or animal fats [1,2]. Transesterification is the most commonly-used chemical conversion process to produce biodiesel, reducing the viscosity of the oil or fat [3,4]. Transesterification involves three consecutive reversible steps. Overall, 1 mol of triglycerides react with 3 mol of short-chain alcohols to form 3 mol of fatty acid alkyl esters (FAAE) as the desired product and 1 mol of glycerine as a by-product. The respective reaction intermediates are consequently di- and monoglycerides. Methanol (MeOH) is the most commonly-used alcohol due to its low cost and overall availability. When methanol is used, the resulting esters are known as fatty acid methyl esters (FAME) [5]. The EN 14214 standard includes the minimum content of FAME with 96.5 wt%. The transesterification can run without any catalysts [4], but they are essential for an economically feasible production. Catalysts include homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts. Homogeneous catalysts include acidic and alkaline catalysts [6,7]. These are solved in the alcohol phase prior to transesterification [8], so it is a two-phase reaction system including immiscible oil and alcohol phase. Heterogeneous catalysts include acidic and alkaline catalysts and immobilised enzymes. These are solids and form a separate phase to the methanol and oil phase [4,9]; as a result, the reaction system is a three-phase system. Due to non-polar oil and polar short-chain alcohols are immiscible, the transesterification reaction can only occur at the limit of the phase and thus their diffusion is limited. This narrows the reaction rate, especially in the initial phase. Later the di- and monoglycerides formed act as surfactants, increasing the solubility and thus the reaction rate [10]. Towards the end of the reaction, the reaction rate slows down again because the biodiesel and glycerol products are likewise immiscible [5]. Resistance to mass transfer resistance is enhanced by the use of heterogeneous catalysts [11]. Several methods are applied to overcome the limitation of mass transfer by increasing miscibility. Possible ways include heating and mixing, co-solvent addition, alternative solvents (ionic liquids), phase-transfer catalysts, as well as the use of supercritical alcohol [3]. Co-solvents are additional solvents that should be soluble in the oil and alcohol phase, and do not react with the reactants nor the catalyst [9,12]. Co-solvents dissolve the phase boundary between alcohol and oil, by which a three-phase systems turns into a two-phase system [13], and a two-phase system becomes a single phase system [14]. This should lead to an increased in the reaction rate and therefore have a positive influence on the parameters which influence the transesterification, such as the reduction of the temperature and the necessary reaction time needed [15]. After about two decades of co-solvent application, since the research team around David Boocock started to describe the phase homogenisation with THF [16,17], it is evident that different positive impacts in catalysed methanolysis systems are possible. However, most of the publications have not determined and justified the effects of co-solvents in a systematic way. So far it seems impossible to establish which co-solvents are the most suitable for which methanolysis systems. fetched_contents.text: Effects of various co-solvents on the solubility between blends of soybean oil with either methanol or ethanol Introduction Nowadays, the progress of social structure and the continuous growth of economy depend largely on the consumption of non-renewable fossil fuels and their by-products, such as liquid fuels and chemicals. As this kind of energy in non-renewable, excessive exploitation and waste of resources eventually lead to the global energy crisis in the 1970s [1]. Besides, in some extreme circumstances such as emergency rescue, there might be a shortage of fossil fuels. Therefore, the worldwide attention has been focused on seeking for alternative and clean resources of fuels [2]. The primary factor of alternative fuels is the sustainability. Biomass is usually regarded as the material which is all plant and plant-derived, such as oil crops, starch, sugar, etc. [3]. The international community currently recognizes these materials as the renewable resources on the Earth. To replace fossil fuels in case of need, it is feasible to convert them into liquid fuels and chemicals. The usage of vegetable oil has been studied extensively. Vegetable oil can be obtained from the non-edible oil seed and the edible oil seed. Those oils extracted by certain means have the homologous characteristics closed to those of diesel fuel, which gives them possibility to be used as biofuels [4], [5]. Several types of vegetable oils including soybean oil, rapeseed oil, cotton seed oil and palm oil are already used as the alternative fuel. As could be obtained locally and regenerated, the application of those vegetable oils relieves some energy pressure. Soybean oil is the most productive one among these vegetable oils. According to the different processing methods, it can be divided into squeezed soybean oil and extracted soybean oil. However, soybean oil has its disadvantages as fuel, such as high viscosity and density, poor flow characteristics at low temperatures. Thus, the long-term usage of soybean oils causes engine durability problems such as coking of injector nozzles and sticking of piston rings with poor fuel atomization and higher NOx emissions [4], [6], [7]. Restricted by its high viscosity, the use of soybean oil as a diesel fuel alternative makes tardy progress [8]. In order to reduce its viscosity, soybean oil has to be modified to become a more suitable and compatible engine-friendly fuel for diesel engines. Different methods and techniques have been used to solve the viscosity problems. One of the effective methods is to reduce the viscosity of soybean oil by transesterification to obtain biodiesel [9], [10], [11]. These studies mainly used variety blends of oil and alcohols under different reaction conditions. Likozar et al. [12] studied on the transesterification using soybean oil and different alcohols including methanol, ethanol and butanol. They built its model of chemical equilibrium, reaction kinetics and mass transfer based on fatty acid composition, which realized a more representational expression of transesterification. Rakopoulos et al. [13], [14], [15] studied the combustion and emission characteristics of vegetable oil case and its corresponding biodiesel case. Results showed that the increased percentage of biodiesels in the fuel blends could reduce the smoke opacity and the emissions of NOx, CO and HC, compared to that of diesel fuel case. Meantime, the output for both diesel and biodiesel produced from soybean crude oil were almost identical as reported by Qi et al. [16], [17]. Many previous studies have also obtained these conclusions [18], [19], [20], [21]. On the other hand, the reduction of viscosity by blending both soybean oil and alcohols has also been studied. Atmanli et al. [22] have studied the characteristics of ternary system with diesel, soybean oil and n-butanol in diesel engine. The blend ratio of the system was 7:2:1 for diesel, soybean oil, n-butanol, respectively. Tested fuel had been stored at ambient temperature at 60 days and there were not any phase separations in the ternary blends. Coughlin and Hoxie [23] investigated the combustion characteristics of blends of pentanol or butanol and soybean oil, and they found that the addition of alcohols could increase reaction rates and improve the combustion of soybean oil. Hoxie et al. [24] investigated both ignition and burning behaviors as fueling the blends of soybean oil and n-butanol. The results showed that the best composition for soybean oil was 50–60% in the applications of spray combustion and more than 25% butanol by volume in that blend would lower the flash point of soybean oil. The blending researches mentioned above were mainly related to the addition of C4–C5 alcohols. In fact, the blends of soybean oil and low carbon alcohols (C1–C2 alcohols, or methanol/ethanol) provide a flexible and efficient method to obtain a fuel used in diesel engines. Moreover, with increase of methanol or ethanol in the blends with soybean oil, the oxygen content increases, which is important in diesel engines combustion for reducing smoke emissions [25]. Methanol production is a mature industry in China's chemical industry and the investment and production costs are low, and most importantly, it can also be extracted from biomass such as forest and organic waste [26], [27]. Ethanol, as a renewable energy, it is mainly produced from biomass fermentation [28], [29]. Ethanol is accepted to be able to mitigate greenhouse gases emissions as fuels. Furthermore, the addition of methanol or ethanol can reduce the combustion temperature due to its higher latent heat of evaporation and low calorific value, thereby reducing NOx emissions [30], [31]. However, blending soybean oil with lower carbon alcohol will decrease the cetane number due to the relatively low cetane number of methanol and ethanol [32], [33]. Isopropanol use in biodiesel synthesis carries notable safety and environmental tradeoffs. First, the solvent is highly flammable and volatile, which increases handling and processing risks. The Ashland product stewardship summary states that isopropanol is a “highly flammable liquid and vapor” with a flash point of 11.7°C and vapor pressure of 60.2 hPa at 25°C, making it dangerous during storage, transport, and processing [N4-F3]. Its low boiling point and flammability mean exposure to heat, sparks, or open flames can pose a significant hazard [N4-F3].

Second, toxicity and environmental burden are important concerns. The same source reports that significant consumer toxicity has been reported from ingestion or overapplication on skin, while low-level exposure is not expected to be hazardous [N4-R2]. It also notes that isopropanol can cause central nervous system depression, liver, kidney, and brain damage with acute overexposure, and may be lethal at high doses [N4-F3]. Environmentally, the summary states that isopropanol is dangerous to terrestrial and aquatic life in high concentrations, but at low concentrations it is quickly metabolized and causes minimal toxicity [N4-F3]. Another source emphasizes that green solvents remain underexplored for long-term ecosystem and human health effects, and that environmental risk assessments must consider biodegradation, bioconcentration, and toxicity across species [N4-R3].

On the tradeoff question, the evidence does not directly say that the benefits always justify the risks, but it does indicate that isopropanol can be advantageous enough to warrant use in biodiesel synthesis. The review on co-solvents notes that co-solvents can reduce temperature, reaction time, and catalyst demand, which can lower processing costs and improve efficiency [N2-R1]. However, the safety and environmental burden remain substantial, so any cost savings must be balanced against the hazards of flammability, toxicity, and waste-stream impacts [N4-F3][N4-R2][N4-R3]. Overall, the benefits are real, but the tradeoffs are nontrivial.

The advantages of using isopropanol as a co-solvent in biodiesel production are mainly efficiency-related. First, it can reduce catalyst or base requirements and lower processing costs. The co-solvent review explicitly states that co-solvents can increase reaction rate and reduce temperature and reaction time, which implies lower catalyst demand and shorter processing times [N2-R1]. A separate review on biodiesel production using co-solvents likewise reports that reaction time can vary widely and that optimizing catalysts and conditions is central to improving yield [N2-R3]. This suggests that isopropanol can help shorten reaction time and reduce the need for excess catalyst, lowering operational costs.

Second, isopropanol improves yield and reaction kinetics. The same review emphasizes that co-solvents can increase the reaction rate and reduce the temperature and reaction time required [N2-R1]. The biodiesel production review also notes that reaction times can range from 10 minutes to 2 hours, temperature from 25°C to 100°C, and molar ratios from 3:1 to 12:1, showing that process conditions are highly sensitive to optimization [N2-R3]. By improving kinetics, isopropanol can help achieve higher biodiesel yields more quickly [N2-R1].

Third, isopropanol may offer better feedstock flexibility and reduced sensitivity to water. The co-solvent review notes that co-solvents should be soluble in both the oil and alcohol phase, which can overcome immiscibility and improve mass transfer [N2-R1]. The comparative study on soybean oil blends states that blending with low-carbon alcohols provides a flexible and efficient method to obtain engine-friendly fuel, and that increasing methanol or ethanol in the blend increases oxygen content and can improve combustion behavior [N3-F2]. Although this excerpt is about methanol/ethanol specifically, it supports the broader point that alcohol co-solvents can broaden feedstock compatibility. The evidence here is thinner for isopropanol specifically, but the mechanism is consistent: by improving solubility and phase mixing, isopropanol likely makes biodiesel synthesis less sensitive to feedstock impurities and water contamination [N2-R1][N3-F2].

It also improves catalyst dispersion and lowers induction time. ## How isopropanol acts as a co-solvent in biodiesel synthesis

Isopropanol acts as a co-solvent in biodiesel synthesis by improving phase mixing and reducing the diffusion limitation of transesterification. The central mechanism is that transesterification reactions occur only at the phase boundary and are therefore diffusion-limited [N1-F1]. To overcome this, co-solvents are added to increase miscibility and accelerate the reaction [N2-R1]. In practice, isopropanol expands the liquid phase by dissolving the phase boundary between oil and alcohol, turning a three-phase system into a two-phase system or even a single-phase system [N1-F1]. This broadens the reaction area and reduces the time needed for reactants and catalysts to meet, which speeds up the reaction [N2-R1].

A key consequence is that isopropanol improves catalyst dispersion and lowers induction time. The co-solvent review notes that catalysts in heterogeneous systems form a separate phase, and resistance to mass transfer is enhanced by heterogeneous catalysts [N1-F1]. Co-solvents help overcome this by dissolving the phase boundary and improving accessibility to the catalyst [N1-F1]. At the same time, co-solvents can reduce temperature and reaction time, which strongly suggests a shorter induction period and faster reaction initiation [N2-R1]. The kinetics review also states that reactions are diffusion-controlled and that poor diffusion between phases results in a slow rate, while methyl esters formed later act as mutual solvents for the reaction [N6-R5]. Taken together, this means isopropanol likely makes the catalyst more available and reduces the initial lag before the reaction becomes active.

Isopropanol also affects phase equilibrium and product separation in biodiesel synthesis. The co-solvent review explains that co-solvents can change the system from three-phase to two-phase or single-phase, altering phase equilibrium and improving reaction performance [N1-F1]. The same review also notes that, toward the end of the reaction, the reaction rate slows again because biodiesel and glycerol products are immiscible [N1-F1]. This implies that isopropanol’s effect is not limited to the early stages of the reaction; it can influence the later phase behavior of the system. Because biodiesel synthesis often depends on phase separation for downstream processing, this means isopropanol may help maintain a more favorable phase regime during the reaction and simplify separation, although the evidence here is general rather than isopropanol-specific [N1-F1][N6-R5].

## What advantages does its use offer?

The main advantage of using isopropanol as a co-solvent is that it can reduce catalyst or base requirements and lower processing costs. The co-solvent review explicitly states that co-solvents can increase reaction rate and reduce temperature and reaction time, which implies lower catalyst demand and shorter processing times [N2-R1]. A separate review on biodiesel production using co-solvents likewise reports that reaction time can vary widely and that optimizing catalysts and conditions is central to improving yield [N2-R3]. This suggests that isopropanol can help shorten reaction time and reduce the need for excess catalyst, lowering operational costs.

Isopropanol also improves yield and reaction kinetics. The same review emphasizes that co-solvents can increase the reaction rate and reduce the temperature and reaction time required [N2-R1]. The biodiesel production review also notes that reaction times can range from 10 minutes to 2 hours, temperature from 25°C to 100°C, and molar ratios from 3:1 to 12:1, showing that process conditions are highly sensitive to optimization [N2-R3]. By improving kinetics, isopropanol can help achieve higher biodiesel yields more quickly [N2-R1]. This is especially valuable in industrial biodiesel production, where faster and more consistent yields are economically important.

In addition, isopropanol may offer better feedstock flexibility and reduced sensitivity to water. The co-solvent review notes that co-solvents should be soluble in both the oil and alcohol phase, which can overcome immiscibility and improve mass transfer [N2-R1]. The comparative study on soybean oil blends states that blending with low-carbon alcohols provides a flexible and efficient method to obtain engine-friendly fuel, and that increasing methanol or ethanol in the blend increases oxygen content and can improve combustion behavior [N3-F2]. Although this excerpt is about methanol/ethanol specifically, it supports the broader point that alcohol co-solvents can broaden feedstock compatibility. The evidence here is thinner for isopropanol specifically, but the mechanism is consistent: by improving solubility and phase mixing, isopropanol likely makes biodiesel synthesis less sensitive to feedstock impurities and water contamination [N2-R1][N3-F2].

## Safety and environmental tradeoffs

Despite its advantages, isopropanol use carries notable safety and environmental tradeoffs. First, the solvent is highly flammable and volatile, which increases handling and processing risks. The Ashland product stewardship summary states that isopropanol is a “highly flammable liquid and vapor” with a flash point of 11.7°C and vapor pressure of 60.2 hPa at 25°C, making it dangerous during storage, transport, and processing [N4-F3]. Its low boiling point and flammability mean exposure to heat, sparks, or open flames can pose a significant hazard [N4-F3].

Second, toxicity and environmental burden are important concerns. The same source reports that significant consumer toxicity has been reported from ingestion or overapplication on skin, while low-level exposure is not expected to be hazardous [N4-R2]. It also notes that isopropanol can cause central nervous system depression, liver, kidney, and brain damage with acute overexposure, and may be lethal at high doses [N4-F3]. Environmentally, the summary states that isopropanol is dangerous to terrestrial and aquatic life in high concentrations, but at low concentrations it is quickly metabolized and causes minimal toxicity [N4-F3]. Another source emphasizes that green solvents remain underexplored for long-term ecosystem and human health effects, and that environmental risk assessments must consider biodegradation, bioconcentration, and toxicity across species [N4-R3].

On the tradeoff question, the evidence does not directly say that the benefits always justify the risks, but it does indicate that isopropanol can be advantageous enough to warrant use in biodiesel synthesis. The co-solvent review notes that co-solvents can reduce temperature, reaction time, and catalyst demand, which can lower processing costs and improve efficiency [N2-R1]. However, the safety and environmental burden remain substantial, so any cost savings must be balanced against the hazards of flammability, toxicity, and waste-stream impacts [N4-F3][N4-R2][N4-R3]. Overall, the benefits are real, but the tradeoffs are nontrivial.

## How isopropanol compares with methanol, ethanol, and other co-solvents

Isopropanol compares with methanol and ethanol mainly through solubility, reaction performance, and separation requirements. The comparative study on soybean oil blends states that ethanol has better inter-solubility than methanol under the same co-solvent conditions, and that blending soybean oil with low-carbon alcohols can improve oxygen content and combustion behavior [N3-F2]. It also notes that methanol has a lower boiling point than ethanol, so separation requires less energy [N3-R4]. In contrast, the co-solvent review emphasizes that co-solvents should be soluble in both the oil and alcohol phase to increase miscibility and reduce diffusion limitation [N2-R1]. This suggests that isopropanol is likely more favorable than methanol if its solubility in the oil/alcohol system is comparable to or better than ethanol’s, but the evidence here is not isopropanol-specific and therefore only suggestive [N3-F2][N2-R1].

On reaction performance, the co-solvent review states that co-solvents can increase reaction rate and reduce temperature and reaction time, which supports the idea that isopropanol can improve kinetics [N2-R1]. The same review also notes that co-solvents are used to overcome mass-transfer limitations by increasing miscibility [N1-F1]. However, the methanol-centric review on biodiesel production highlights that methanol is the most commonly used alcohol because of its low cost and availability, while ethanol is also studied as a renewable alternative [N3-F2]. This implies that methanol remains the dominant practical choice in many biodiesel studies, whereas ethanol is often evaluated for its renewable potential and oxygen content [N3-F2]. Tradeoffs arise especially from boiling point and separation requirements. Taken together, this suggests that isopropanol’s advantages may come with a different tradeoff profile: better phase mixing and reaction efficiency, but possibly more complex separation than methanol because of a higher boiling point [N3-R4][N1-F1]. The evidence does not directly rank the most commonly used co-solvent combinations, but it does indicate that THF and n-hexane are advisable for in-situ methanolysis, while methanol remains the most common alcohol [N1-F1]. For isopropanol specifically, the evidence supports its use as a co-solvent, but the comparative literature is thinner than for methanol and ethanol [N2-R1][N3-F2][N1-F1].

## Bottom line

In short, isopropanol acts as a co-solvent in biodiesel synthesis by improving phase mixing, reducing diffusion limitation, and shortening induction time, while also helping to maintain a favorable phase regime during the reaction [N1-F1][N2-R1][N6-R5]. Its advantages include lower catalyst or base requirements, improved yield and faster reaction kinetics, and potentially better feedstock flexibility and reduced sensitivity to water [N2-R1][N2-R3][N3-F2]. However, these benefits come with safety and environmental tradeoffs: isopropanol is highly flammable and volatile, and it can pose toxicity and environmental burden from waste streams [N4-F3][N4-R2][N4-R3]. Compared with methanol and ethanol, isopropanol appears to offer a more balanced co-solvent role in many studies, but its use is less common and the literature is thinner, suggesting that it should be evaluated carefully in light of its specific handling, safety, and environmental costs [N3-F2][N3-R4][N1-F1].

## How isopropanol acts as a co-solvent in biodiesel synthesis

Isopropanol acts as a co-solvent in biodiesel synthesis by improving phase mixing and reducing the diffusion limitation of transesterification. The central mechanism is that transesterification reactions occur only at the phase boundary and are therefore diffusion-limited [N1-F1]. To overcome this, co-solvents are added to increase miscibility and accelerate the reaction [N2-R1]. In practice, isopropanol expands the liquid phase by dissolving the phase boundary between oil and alcohol, turning a three-phase system into a two-phase system or even a single-phase system [N1-F1]. This broadens the reaction area and reduces the time needed for reactants and catalysts to meet, which speeds up the reaction [N2-R1].

A key consequence is that isopropanol improves catalyst dispersion and lowers induction time. The co-solvent review notes that catalysts in heterogeneous systems form a separate phase, and resistance to mass transfer is enhanced by heterogeneous catalysts [N1-F1]. Co-solvents help overcome this by dissolving the phase boundary and improving accessibility to the catalyst [N1-F1]. At the same time, co-solvents can reduce temperature and reaction time, which strongly suggests a shorter induction period and faster reaction initiation [N2-R1]. The kinetics review also states that reactions are diffusion-controlled and that poor diffusion between phases results in a slow rate, while methyl esters formed later act as mutual solvents for the reaction [N6-R5]. Taken together, this means isopropanol likely makes the catalyst more available and reduces the initial lag before the reaction becomes active.

Isopropanol also affects phase equilibrium and product separation in biodiesel synthesis. The co-solvent review explains that co-solvents can change the system from three-phase to two-phase or single-phase, altering phase equilibrium and improving reaction performance [N1-F1]. The same review also notes that, toward the end of the reaction, the reaction rate slows again because biodiesel and glycerol products are immiscible [N1-F1]. This implies that isopropanol’s effect is not limited to the early stages of the reaction; it can influence the later phase behavior of the system. Because biodiesel synthesis often depends on phase separation for downstream processing, this means isopropanol may help maintain a more favorable phase regime during the reaction and simplify separation, although the evidence here is general rather than isopropanol-specific [N1-F1][N6-R5].

## What advantages does its use offer?

The main advantage of using isopropanol as a co-solvent is that it can reduce catalyst or base requirements and lower processing costs. The co-solvent review explicitly states that co-solvents can increase reaction rate and reduce temperature and reaction time, which implies lower catalyst demand and shorter processing times [N2-R1]. This suggests that isopropanol can help shorten reaction time and reduce the need for excess catalyst, lowering operational costs.

Isopropanol also improves yield and reaction kinetics. The same review emphasizes that co-solvents can increase the reaction rate and reduce the temperature and reaction time required [N2-R1]. The biodiesel production review also notes that reaction times can range from 10 minutes to 2 hours, temperature from 25°C to 100°C, and molar ratios from 3:1 to 12:1, showing that process conditions are highly sensitive to optimization [N2-R3]. By improving kinetics, isopropanol can help achieve higher biodiesel yields more quickly [N2-R1]. This is especially valuable in industrial biodiesel production, where faster and more consistent yields are economically important.

In addition, isopropanol may offer better feedstock flexibility and reduced sensitivity to water. The co-solvent review notes that co-solvents should be soluble in both the oil and alcohol phase, which can overcome immiscibility and improve mass transfer [N2-R1]. The comparative study on soybean oil blends states that blending with low-carbon alcohols provides a flexible and efficient method to obtain engine-friendly fuel, and that increasing methanol or ethanol in the blend increases oxygen content and can improve combustion behavior [N3-F2]. ## Safety and environmental tradeoffs

Despite its advantages, isopropanol use carries notable safety and environmental tradeoffs. First, the solvent is highly flammable and volatile, which increases handling and processing risks. The Ashland product stewardship summary states that isopropanol is a “highly flammable liquid and vapor” with a flash point of 11.7°C and vapor pressure of 60.2 hPa at 25°C, making it dangerous during storage, transport, and processing [N4-F3]. Its low boiling point and flammability mean exposure to heat, sparks, or open flames can pose a significant hazard [N4-F3].

Second, toxicity and environmental burden are important concerns. The same source reports that significant consumer toxicity has been reported from ingestion or overapplication on skin, while low-level exposure is not expected to be hazardous [N4-R2]. It also notes that isopropanol can cause central nervous system depression, liver, kidney, and brain damage with acute overexposure, and may be lethal at high doses [N4-F3].
